questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with newly diagnosed lung cancer undergoes a full staging workup. The report lists a 3-cm primary tumor, involvement of two regional lymph nodes, grade 3 (anaplastic) histology, and a solitary lesion in the liver consistent with tumor spread. Which of the following findings most strongly worsens her prognosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tumor that is well vascularized

choices.label: B
choices.text: Involvement of two regional lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 3-cm size of the primary tumor

explanation.summary: Distant metastasis (the M in TNM) is the single most important component of staging and confers the worst prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Of the three TNM components, metastasis is the most important prognostic factor, and spread to a distant organ such as the liver carries the worst outlook. It outweighs tumor size, nodal spread, and grade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vascularity of the tumor is not one of the prognostic parameters emphasized in staging and grading.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nodal involvement (N) ranks below metastasis in prognostic weight; two nodes is less severe than distant spread.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tumor size (T) is the least important of the three TNM components and is far less ominous than distant spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Grade is an important prognostic factor but is explicitly less important than stage, and metastasis dominates staging.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man completes chemotherapy for lymphoma. On follow-up, his physical exam, blood work, and imaging show no evidence of cancer, and the oncologist says he is in complete remission. Which of the following best describes what this means?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All signs and symptoms of the cancer have disappeared

choices.label: B
choices.text: Imaging shows no growth of the original tumor, though symptoms persist

choices.label: C
choices.text: Signs and symptoms are alleviated but not eliminated

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cancer has been definitively cured and cannot return

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor is at least 50% smaller than before treatment

explanation.summary: Complete remission means all evidence, signs, and symptoms of cancer have disappeared, but it is not the same as cure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complete remission means no cancer is detectable on physical exam, blood work, or imaging. It is distinguished from cure because undetected cancer cells may still remain and could regrow.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Imaging showing no growth of the original tumor with residual disease describes partial remission, not complete remission.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Signs and symptoms alleviated but not eliminated defines partial remission.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Providers avoid the word cure because undetected cells may persist even in complete remission; complete remission is not a guarantee of cure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A tumor at least 50% smaller but still present is a criterion for partial remission, not complete remission.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. Her oncologist tells her that, based on her diagnosis, 75% of patients with her cancer will not die as a result of their cancer within 5 years of diagnosis. Which parameter is the oncologist using to describe her prognosis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: 5-year relative survival versus a matched population

explanation.summary: Cancer-specific survival counts only deaths caused by the cancer itself over a set period after diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer-specific survival is the percentage of patients with a specific type and stage who have not died as a result of that specific cancer in a given period after diagnosis. That is exactly what the oncologist described.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Disease-free survival is the percentage with no signs of cancer during a period after completing treatment, not deaths from the cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Overall survival counts patients who have not died from any cause, not just the cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Relative survival compares survival of patients with cancer to a matched cancer-free population.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The oncologist specified a 5-year window and death from the cancer, not a 10-year overall figure.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A biopsy of a breast mass is reviewed by a pathologist. Which of the following histologic descriptions most likely corresponds to a high-grade cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cells that form glands and resemble normal breast tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extensive tumor infiltration into adjacent tissue and lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Poorly differentiated cells with numerous mitoses

explanation.summary: Grade reflects histology; high-grade tumors are poorly differentiated or anaplastic with marked nuclear atypia and abundant mitoses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Grade describes the histologic appearance and number of mitoses. High-grade (poorly differentiated or anaplastic) cancers lack differentiation, show pleomorphic nuclei, and have numerous mitotic figures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cells that form glands and resemble normal tissue describe a well-differentiated, low-grade tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum tumor marker levels are not a component of grade, which is based on microscopic appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infiltration into adjacent tissue and lymph nodes reflects stage (extent of spread), not grade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Well-differentiated cells with uniform nuclei describe a low-grade, not a high-grade, cancer.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has an elevated serum CA19-9 detected during evaluation of abdominal pain and weight loss. An elevation of this tumor marker is most classically associated with which of the following cancers?

explanation.summary: CA19-9 is a tumor marker associated with colon and pancreatic cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: CA19-9 is classically elevated in pancreatic cancer (and colon cancer). In a patient with abdominal pain and weight loss, a high CA19-9 points toward pancreatic cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatocellular carcinoma is marked by alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), not CA19-9.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neuroendocrine tumors are associated with chromogranin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ovarian cancer is associated with CA-125.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostate cancer is associated with prostate-specific antigen (PSA).

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with non-small cell lung cancer is assigned a stage of T2 N1 M1. Which single feature of his cancer carries the greatest weight in determining his prognosis?

choices.label: C
choices.text: The moderate differentiation of the tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: The N1 involvement of one lymph node

explanation.summary: Among the three TNM components, metastasis (M) is the most important prognostic factor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The M component describes distant spread and is the most important of the three TNM factors. M1 (metastasis present) therefore weighs most heavily on prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tumor markers help track response and recurrence but are not the dominant prognostic component of TNM staging.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Grade (differentiation) is a prognostic factor but is less important than stage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nodal involvement (N) is important and second to metastasis, but still ranks below M.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor size (T) is the least important of the three TNM components.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is diagnosed with stage 3B non-small cell lung cancer. Using the staging-based survival data, which of the following is closest to her expected 5-year survival rate?

explanation.summary: Higher stage means worse prognosis; stage 3B non-small cell lung cancer has roughly a 5% 5-year survival.
explanation.whyCorrect: The stage-specific survival table lists a 5-year survival of about 5% for stage 3B non-small cell lung cancer, illustrating how advancing stage sharply lowers survival.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1% corresponds to stage 4 (metastatic) disease, worse than stage 3B.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 14% corresponds to stage 3A disease, one substage below 3B.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 49% corresponds to stage 1A disease, much earlier than stage 3B.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A researcher reports that, for a particular cancer, a given statistic represents the percentage of patients with that cancer type and stage who have not died from any cause within 5 years of diagnosis. Which survival measure is being described?

explanation.summary: Overall survival counts patients who have not died from any cause during a set period after diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Overall survival is the percentage of patients with a specific type and stage of cancer who have not died from any cause in a certain period after diagnosis, which matches the description exactly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cancer-specific survival counts only deaths caused by the cancer, not deaths from any cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disease-free survival tracks the absence of cancer signs after completing treatment, not death from any cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progression-free interval is not one of the survival measures defined in the source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relative survival compares patients with cancer against a matched cancer-free population.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man treated for colorectal carcinoma had a carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level that normalized after surgery. During surveillance, his CEA begins to rise steadily on serial measurements. Which of the following does this trend most likely suggest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A normal age-related change in the marker

choices.label: B
choices.text: A positive response to ongoing treatment

choices.label: E
choices.text: That the patient is now cured

explanation.summary: After a baseline is established following treatment, a rising tumor marker suggests cancer recurrence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor markers are useful for monitoring after treatment. Once a post-treatment baseline is set, a later increase in the marker suggests the cancer has returned.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The PSA example, not CEA, is the marker described as changing with age; a steady rise here reflects disease, not aging.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A decrease in a tumor marker, not an increase, signifies a positive treatment response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complete remission requires no detectable cancer; a rising marker indicates the opposite.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A rising marker argues against cure; providers are already reluctant to use the term cure.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with advanced cancer has progressive weakness, loss of appetite, and marked muscle wasting with more than 5% loss of body weight despite adequate nutrition offered. This hypercatabolic state is thought to account for roughly 30% of cancer deaths. Which of the following mediators are most implicated in this process?

explanation.summary: Cancer cachexia is a hypercatabolic wasting state driven by inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6.
explanation.whyCorrect: The picture describes cancer cachexia, a hypercatabolic state with loss of muscle mass that occurs in about half of cancer patients and contributes to roughly 30% of cancer deaths. Inflammatory mediators including TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 are implicated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AFP and CEA are tumor markers, not cytokines driving cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen and progesterone are hormones related to breast cancer biology, not drivers of cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin and glucagon regulate glucose metabolism and are not the implicated inflammatory mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PSA and CA-125 are tumor markers, not mediators of the wasting process.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman receives chemotherapy for cancer. Follow-up imaging shows her tumor burden has decreased by about 60% with no new lesions, but residual tumor is still present and blood tests remain mildly abnormal. Which of the following terms best describes her current status?

explanation.summary: Partial remission means the cancer responded to treatment and shrank, but signs of disease remain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Partial remission means signs and symptoms are alleviated but not eliminated; imaging showing tumors at least 50% smaller and not growing, with residual disease, fits partial remission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cancer-specific survival is a population survival statistic, not a status for an individual's tumor response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complete remission requires that all evidence, signs, and symptoms have disappeared, but residual tumor remains here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cure means no trace of cancer at all, which is not the case with visible residual tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Disease-free survival is a survival statistic measured after treatment completion, not a description of current tumor response.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer, and molecular testing is performed to help refine her prognosis. Which of the following receptor profiles is associated with the most favorable prognosis?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Presence of both BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations

explanation.summary: In breast cancer, estrogen receptor-positive and HER2/Neu-negative tumors carry a better prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Molecular characteristics influence prognosis: estrogen receptor-positive breast cancers carry a better prognosis than receptor-negative ones, and HER2/Neu-negative cancers carry a better prognosis than HER2/Neu-positive ones. The combination of both favorable features is the most favorable profile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estrogen receptor-negative removes the favorable receptor feature, worsening prognosis relative to receptor-positive disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen receptor-negative and HER2/Neu-positive combines two unfavorable features and has a worse prognosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HER2/Neu-positive status is unfavorable and offsets the benefit of being receptor-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations are molecular features that can worsen prognosis and are not the favorable receptor profile described.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman undergoes biopsy of a breast lesion. Malignant-appearing epithelial cells fill several ducts, but the thin connective tissue layer separating the duct epithelium from the underlying stroma is intact in every section examined. Which additional finding on deeper sections would reclassify this lesion as an invasive carcinoma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of normal polarity of the duct-lining cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marked nuclear pleomorphism of the ductal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Numerous mitotic figures within the involved ducts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tumor cells extending into many neighboring ducts and lobules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor cells penetrating through the basement membrane

explanation.summary: In epithelial malignancies, invasion is defined by penetration through the basement membrane; a cancer that has not done so is in situ.
explanation.whyCorrect: The basement membrane is the thin connective tissue layer separating epithelium from the underlying tissue. A cancer is in situ when it does not penetrate the basement membrane, and invasion is defined by penetration through it. Only invasive cancers have the ability to metastasize.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Disordered polarity within the epithelium does not mean the basement membrane has been breached.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nuclear atypia is consistent with malignancy but does not establish penetration of the basement membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proliferative activity confined above an intact basement membrane does not define invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spread within additional ducts keeps the cells above the basement membrane, so the lesion remains in situ.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a poorly defined breast mass. Biopsy shows small, discohesive tumor cells infiltrating the stroma in single-file lines with loss of normal architecture. An immunostain for a cell-cell adhesion protein that is normally present on breast epithelium shows no staining in the tumor cells. Loss of which protein most directly explains this infiltrative pattern?

explanation.summary: Invasive lobular carcinoma downregulates E-cadherin, so cells separate easily and infiltrate in single file.
explanation.whyCorrect: Invasion begins when cancers separate cells by disrupting E-cadherin or catenins. Breast adenocarcinomas, particularly lobular carcinoma, downregulate E-cadherin, which makes it easier to separate the cells from one another; invasive lobular carcinoma shows loss of architecture, single-file infiltration and absent E-cadherin staining.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HER2 is a growth-signaling receptor targeted by trastuzumab, not the adhesion protein lost in lobular carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Laminin receptors are often overexpressed (not lost) by cancer cells and mediate binding to basement membrane, not cell-cell cohesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tubulin forms microtubules of the mitotic spindle; it does not hold epithelial cells together.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF drives angiogenesis; it is not a cell-cell adhesion protein.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon. Staging CT shows multiple new nodules in the liver, and biopsy of one confirms metastatic colonic adenocarcinoma. Which factor best explains why the liver was the site of these metastases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arterial spread of tumor cells through the hepatic artery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chemokine receptors that home tumor cells to hepatocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphatic flow from the colon into hepatic lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seeding of tumor cells across the peritoneal cavity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venous drainage of the colon passing first to the liver

explanation.summary: Colon cancer typically metastasizes to the liver because the liver is the first downstream organ of the colon's portal venous drainage.
explanation.whyCorrect: One key factor determining where circulating tumor cells end up is the location and vascular drainage of the primary tumor. All portal blood from the colon drains into the liver, so tumor cells lodge in the first capillary bed they reach there; the lecture gives colon-to-liver spread as the example of this anatomic factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arterial spread is the less common hematogenous route because arterial walls are thick and elastin-rich.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chemokine-receptor tropism is a separate factor; the lecture attributes colon-to-liver spread to vascular drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The liver is reached through portal venous blood, not through lymphatic drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peritoneal seeding produces surface implants in the cavity (as with ovarian carcinoma), not drainage-based liver deposits.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is found to have a solid renal mass on imaging, and biopsy shows renal cell carcinoma. Unlike the usual pattern for tumors of epithelial origin, this tumor is classically known for which pattern of spread?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphatic spread to regional lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seeding of tumor cells across the pleural cavity

explanation.summary: Renal cell carcinoma is one of four carcinomas known for hematogenous rather than lymphatic spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most carcinomas spread lymphatically, but four are known for spreading hematogenously: follicular thyroid carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatic spread is the typical carcinoma route, which renal cell carcinoma is a notable exception to.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peritoneal seeding is the classic pattern of ovarian carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pleural seeding is a seeding route, not the characteristic route of renal cell carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subarachnoid seeding is the pattern of glioblastoma within the brain and spinal cord.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has an enlarging deep mass in the thigh. Biopsy shows a malignant tumor of mesenchymal origin. By which route is this type of tumor most typically associated with spreading?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seeding across an adjacent joint cavity

explanation.summary: Sarcomas (mesenchymal tumors) are associated with hematogenous spread; carcinomas with lymphatic spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sarcomas are of mesenchymal origin and are associated with hematogenous spread, whereas epithelial carcinomas are associated with lymphatic spread. This is a tendency rather than a fixed rule, but it is the typical association.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spread along epithelial surfaces is not one of the three main metastatic pathways described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic spread is the pattern associated with carcinomas, not sarcomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Joint cavities are among the open spaces where seeding can occur, but seeding is not the typical sarcoma route.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peritoneal seeding is classic for ovarian carcinoma.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman undergoes lumpectomy for invasive ductal carcinoma. Sections show tumor aggregates inside dilated lymphatic channels at the tumor edge and within a regional lymph node, but no tumor within blood vessels. Which property of lymphatic vessels best explains why carcinoma cells commonly enter them rather than blood vessels?

choices.label: B
choices.text: They carry rapid, high-shear flow that pulls cells in

choices.label: C
choices.text: They drain directly into the portal venous system

choices.label: D
choices.text: They have thick walls with abundant elastin

choices.label: E
choices.text: They lack tight junctions and a basement membrane

explanation.summary: Lymphatic intravasation is mostly mechanical: lymphatics are low-shear and lack the tight junctions and basement membrane of blood vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lymphatic pathway is a low-shear system that does not have the tight junctions and basement membrane associated with blood vessels, making it easier for a tumor cell to get into a lymphatic vessel than into a blood vessel. This mechanical ease is why carcinomas such as breast cancer typically spread lymphatically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Laminin receptors are overexpressed by cancer cells, not by lymphatic endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatics are a low-shear system; shear stress kills circulating tumor cells rather than helping them enter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Portal venous drainage explains liver metastasis from the colon, stomach and pancreas, not lymphatic entry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thick elastin-rich walls describe arteries and make them harder, not easier, to penetrate.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman has progressive abdominal distension. At surgery, an ovarian carcinoma is found, along with numerous tumor nodules studding the omentum and the surfaces of the abdominal organs. By which mechanism did this tumor most likely reach these sites?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous spread through the portal vein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seeding of tumor cells across a body cavity

explanation.summary: Ovarian carcinoma is known for seeding the peritoneal cavity, including the omentum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Seeding requires an open space such as the peritoneal cavity, pleural cavity, subarachnoid space or joint cavities, in which tumor cells are sown much as a gardener sows seeds. Ovarian carcinoma is the lecture's example of seeding the peritoneal cavity, with omental involvement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arterial spread is uncommon and would not produce diffuse surface implants within a cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Portal venous spread delivers tumor to the liver parenchyma, not to omental and serosal surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic spread produces nodal metastases, not implants across the peritoneal surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subarachnoid seeding is how glioblastoma spreads within the brain and spinal cord.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with a malignancy begins a chemotherapy regimen that includes methotrexate. Which molecular target does this drug directly inhibit to interfere with DNA synthesis?

explanation.summary: Methotrexate, an S-phase antimetabolite, inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and blocks formation of reduced folates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methotrexate binds to and inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, inhibiting the formation of reduced folates, and thymidylate synthetase, resulting in inhibition of purine and thymidylic acid synthesis. This interferes with DNA synthesis, repair and cellular replication in the S phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD20 on B cells is the target of rituximab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA polymerase inhibition is the primary action of cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The topoisomerase I-DNA complex is the target of irinotecan.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tubulin is the target of the microtubule inhibitors (vinca alkaloids and taxanes).

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is started on a taxane. Her oncologist explains that, although this drug and the vinca alkaloids both act on microtubules during mitosis, their effects on microtubules differ. Which mechanism characterizes the taxane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds tubulin and blocks formation of new microtubules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-links DNA strands regardless of cycle phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits DNA polymerase after DNA incorporation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stabilizes microtubules and blocks their disassembly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traps topoisomerase I and blocks DNA religation

explanation.summary: Taxanes promote and stabilize microtubules and prevent their disassembly; vinca alkaloids block microtubule formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Taxanes promote microtubule assembly by enhancing the action of tubulin dimers, stabilizing existing microtubules and inhibiting their disassembly, which interferes with mitosis. The vinca alkaloids do the opposite at the same target: they bind tubulin and inhibit microtubule formation, arresting cells at metaphase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking microtubule formation describes the vinca alkaloids, the contrast drug in the stem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phase-independent DNA cross-linking describes the alkylating and platinum agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA polymerase inhibition after incorporation into DNA describes cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trapping topoisomerase I and blocking religation describes irinotecan.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with bladder cancer is treated with cisplatin. Which pairing correctly describes this drug's mechanism and its relationship to the cell cycle?

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA strand breakage; specific to G2 phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate antagonism; specific to S phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spindle disruption; specific to M phase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topoisomerase I block; specific to S phase

explanation.summary: Platinum agents, like alkylating agents, cross-link DNA chains and act independently of the cell cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alkylating agents operate independently of the cell cycle, cross-linking DNA chains and causing them to break, which inhibits DNA replication and transcription. The same mechanism is observed in the platinum agents carboplatin and cisplatin, used in cancers including bladder cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA strand breakage in G2 phase describes bleomycin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate antagonism in S phase describes methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spindle disruption in M phase describes the microtubule inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman has invasive breast carcinoma. Testing shows the tumor is estrogen receptor-negative and strongly HER2-positive. Which agent directly targets the receptor that is overexpressed by her tumor?

explanation.summary: Trastuzumab binds HER2 receptors and is primarily used for HER2-positive breast cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trastuzumab binds to HER2 receptors on tumor cells, blocking the signaling pathways that drive growth and marking the cells for immune-mediated destruction. It is primarily used for HER2-positive breast cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bevacizumab binds VEGF to inhibit angiogenesis rather than a receptor on the tumor cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CAR-T cells are a cell therapy, not an agent described as targeting HER2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells and is used for B-cell malignancies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tamoxifen is a SERM used for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer; this tumor is ER-negative.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy for lung cancer develops persistent nausea and vomiting, and a routine blood count shows marked decreases in all cell lines. His sister, treated with a monoclonal antibody for a different cancer, had far fewer adverse effects. Which feature of his drugs best accounts for both of his adverse effects?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of tumor angiogenesis through VEGF

choices.label: C
choices.text: Preferential injury to cells resting in G0

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selective binding to tumor surface receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxicity to rapidly dividing normal cells

explanation.summary: Most cytotoxic drugs target any rapidly dividing cell, so gastric mucosa (nausea/vomiting) and bone marrow (myelosuppression) are injured.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because most chemotherapeutic drugs target any rapidly dividing cell, not just cancer cells, they also kill normal cells that turn over rapidly. Drugs affecting gastric mucosa lead to nausea and vomiting, and drugs affecting bone marrow cause myelosuppression. More specific agents such as monoclonal antibodies act in a targeted way, reducing the number and intensity of adverse effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune checkpoints are pathways tumors use to turn off immunity; cytotoxic drugs do not act by activating them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: VEGF blockade is the mechanism of bevacizumab, not of cytotoxic chemotherapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cells in G0 are nondividing; cytotoxic toxicity falls on rapidly cycling cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selective receptor binding is the property of targeted monoclonal antibodies and explains their milder toxicity.

questions.topicName: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview
